title: Polycrisis Resilience: The Global South
subtitle: How accelerated human development can become an instrument of polycrisis mitigation across Africa, Asia and beyond
description: How economic convergence, technology diffusion, clean energy and institutional capacity can reduce exposure to interconnected risks across Africa, Asia and beyond.
contribution: Applies the concept to the Global South through an eight-mechanism resilience architecture, the development-resilience spiral and development-risk trap, and the Development Resilience Dividend.
abstract: This report introduces a development-centered framework for understanding and strengthening Polycrisis Resilience in the Global South. It argues that resilience is not built solely through emergency response, preparedness, or climate adaptation, but also through accelerated human development. The central proposition is that economic convergence, technology diffusion, sustainable development, and institutional capacity-building are not merely development objectives. They are mechanisms for reducing human exposure and vulnerability to interconnected global risks. The report contends that improvements in income, infrastructure, health, education, clean energy, governance, and social stability can simultaneously address multiple overlapping threats, including climate change, poverty, disease, pollution, conflict, and infrastructure deficits.

To operationalize this concept, the report presents the Global South Polycrisis Resilience Architecture, an integrated framework consisting of eight mutually reinforcing development mechanisms: economic convergence, technology diffusion, clean transition, infrastructure, human development, climate adaptation, institutional capacity, and conflict resilience. The framework emphasizes that resilience emerges from the interaction of these mechanisms rather than from isolated interventions, creating either a development-resilience spiral or, when neglected, a development-risk trap.

Drawing on evidence from development, health, climate, energy, and disaster-risk research, the report examines how development has already reduced vulnerability through improved health outcomes, declining disaster mortality, expanded access to technology, and strengthened adaptive capacity. It identifies finance and the cost of capital as critical constraints on resilience-building efforts and highlights the potential advantages of technology diffusion and latecomer development pathways across Africa, Asia, and other emerging regions. The report also introduces the concept of a Development Resilience Dividend, a proposed framework for measuring reductions in human suffering, premature mortality, exposure, and systemic vulnerability attributable to accelerated development interventions relative to credible counterfactuals.

The report concludes that the Global South will play a decisive role in shaping humanity's ability to navigate the twenty-first century polycrisis. While development alone cannot eliminate risk, it can substantially reduce vulnerability and increase adaptive capacity when paired with climate adaptation, institutional strengthening, and sustainable technologies. The central finding is that development should be viewed not only as an outcome of resilience policy but also as one of its most powerful instruments.
coreProposition: Convergence, technological diffusion, sustainable development and institutional capacity-building are not merely economic objectives. They are mechanisms for reducing human exposure to interconnected global risks.

keyFindings.title: Development deficits are resilience deficits.
keyFindings.text: Most of the gaps that define the Global South, in health coverage, sanitation, water, connectivity, energy and income, are also the conditions that turn hazards into disasters. Billions are exposed on several fronts at once.

keyFindings.title: Eight development mechanisms carry the strategy:
keyFindings.text: economic convergence, technology diffusion, clean transition, infrastructure, human development, climate adaptation, institutional capacity and conflict resilience. Each reduces exposure or vulnerability directly, and each also strengthens the others.

keyFindings.title: The mechanisms are interdependent.
keyFindings.text: In H Heuristics' qualitative assessment, 19 of 56 possible links between mechanisms are rated high-strength. Institutional capacity, economic convergence and infrastructure reach the most others. The same links can run in reverse, producing a development-risk trap.

keyFindings.title: Development has already reduced risk at scale.
keyFindings.text: Cyclone deaths in Bangladesh and Odisha fell by orders of magnitude between the 1970s and 2010s as warning systems, shelters and rural income improved, and under-five mortality has fallen by more than half since 2000.

keyFindings.title: Latecomers can move faster than pioneers.
keyFindings.text: Africa's solar module imports rose about 60% in the year to June 2025, and mobile technology helped lift women's account ownership in low- and middle-income countries from 37% to 73% between 2011 and 2024.

keyFindings.title: Finance is the binding constraint.
keyFindings.text: The gap between adaptation needs and flows is 12 to 14 times current flows, debt service now exceeds what many countries spend on health or education, and the cost of capital for clean projects in emerging and developing economies is more than twice that in advanced ones.

keyFindings.title: Growth does not automatically produce resilience.
keyFindings.text: Growth that places assets and people in floodplains, locks in pollution or concentrates gains can increase exposure. The framework evaluates development by what it does to risk, not by its pace alone.

keyFindings.title: The combination matters most.
keyFindings.text: In a stylized model, an integrated scenario that pairs development with adaptation, health and institutions ends 2050 with a vulnerability index of 75, against 148 for growth alone and 161 for stalled development.

glossary.definition: The ability of people, institutions and systems to adjust to changing conditions, take advantage of opportunities and cope with consequences.
The spread of failure or stress from one system to others through dependencies.
The shift from pollution-intensive and inefficient systems toward cleaner energy, industry, transportation, agriculture and infrastructure.
The process by which poorer economies close the gap in income, productivity and capability with richer ones.
The return that investors require to finance a project; higher costs make capital-intensive projects less viable.
An estimate of what would have happened without an intervention, used to measure its effect.
A reinforcing loop in which low income and weak infrastructure produce losses that prevent investment in capacity (H Heuristics).
A reinforcing loop in which investment in capability raises income and capacity, lowering exposure and enabling further investment (H Heuristics).
The reduction in human suffering, premature mortality, exposure and systemic vulnerability attributable to accelerated development, relative to a credible counterfactual (H Heuristics).
A system that monitors hazards, forecasts their impact, communicates warnings and prompts action.
The people, assets and systems located where hazards can affect them.
A shorthand for low- and middle-income countries in Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Caribbean and the Pacific; not a precise category.
The ability of public organizations to govern, finance, deliver services and implement plans.
A pattern in which middle-income economies fail to move to high income, often stalling at about a tenth of US income per person.
A cluster of related crises in several global systems that interact so that the overall impact exceeds the sum of the parts.

The capacity of people, communities, economies, institutions and systems to anticipate, withstand, adapt to, recover from and reduce the cascading effects of multiple interconnected crises (H Heuristics).
The spread of proven technologies beyond the places that invented them.
The degree to which people and systems are harmed when a hazard strikes.
